lessons.title: Plants: making food, pollination and seed dispersal

objectives: Describe pollination and how seeds are spread.
Put the stages of a plant's life cycle in order.
reviewNotes: Photosynthesis described at the simple level; check whether chlorophyll and pollination are expected in Class 5.

blocks.title: Making food
blocks.md: Green leaves contain **chlorophyll**, which gives them their colour. Using **sunlight**, leaves turn **carbon dioxide** (from the air) and **water** (from the soil) into **food** (sugar) and give out **oxygen**. This is **photosynthesis**. The food is used for growth and stored in roots, stems, fruits and seeds, for example in cassava and yam.

blocks.caption: Life cycle of a flowering plant.
blocks.alt: Five boxes joined by arrows: seed, seedling, plant, flower, fruit.

blocks.title: Pollination and seeds
blocks.md: **Pollination** is the moving of **pollen** from one flower to the **stigma** of a flower of the same kind, by **insects** (bees, butterflies) or by the **wind**. After pollination the flower can make **seeds** inside a **fruit**. Seeds are spread (**dispersed**) by **wind** (light, winged or fluffy seeds), **water** (coconut), **animals** (sticky burrs, fruit eaten and dropped) or by the **pod bursting open** (beans).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that plants take in oxygen to make food: they take in **carbon dioxide** (they also breathe like all living things).
- Thinking that soil is the plant's food: the food is made in the leaves.
- Thinking that pollination and seed dispersal are the same.
- Forgetting that seeds are spread so that new plants do not crowd the parent.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Name three things a leaf needs to make food and one thing it gives out.
steps: It needs sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.
blocks.answer: Needs sunlight, water, carbon dioxide; gives out oxygen.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A coconut falls into a river and lands on a beach far away. How was the seed dispersed?
steps: The seed floated and was carried by the water.

objectives: Build a food chain and name producers and consumers.
Say where energy in a food chain comes from.
Give examples of how animals are adapted to their habitats.
reviewNotes: The chain examples are generic and not claimed as exact Cameroon food webs.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Food chains
blocks.md: A **food chain** shows who eats whom. **Plants** are **producers**: they make their own food using sunlight. Animals are **consumers**: **herbivores** (primary consumers) eat plants; **carnivores** (secondary consumers) eat other animals. The arrow means 'is eaten by'. **Decomposers** (bacteria, fungi, some insects) break down dead plants and animals.

blocks.caption: A food chain: maize, rat, snake, eagle.
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: maize, rat, snake, eagle.

blocks.title: Energy and adaptation
blocks.md: The **Sun** is the first source of energy: plants capture it and pass it on along the chain. An **adaptation** is a feature that helps an animal to live in its habitat: a **fish** has gills and fins for water; a **bird** has wings and light bones to fly; a **chameleon** changes colour to hide; a **lion** has sharp teeth for eating meat. A **food web** joins many food chains.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Drawing the arrow the wrong way: the arrow goes **from the food to the eater** (maize → rat).
- Forgetting that every food chain starts with a plant.
- Thinking that animals choose to change their bodies: adaptations develop over many generations.
- Putting a herbivore after a carnivore in a chain.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: In the chain grass → grasshopper → bird → hawk, name the producer and the top consumer.
steps: The producer is the plant that makes food: grass.
The last animal in the chain is the hawk.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: What happens to the rats if all the snakes in a field are killed?
steps: Fewer animals eat the rats, so the rat numbers may increase.
They may then eat too much of the maize.
blocks.answer: The number of rats may grow and damage the crops.
